name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,220

indicators.note: something breaking into a thing gets inside it, so one piece is pushed into the middle of another

blocks.note: the Los Angeles Police Department's initials, taken as written
a sash is the frame holding the glass of a window

explanation.surface: Sloppy Los Angeles police officers smash their way through a door frame.
explanation.walkthrough: The police force's initials are taken literally and sit inside the window frame, SLAPDASH.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done in a hurried, sloppy way without proper care is described with this informal adjective.

clue.text: Young actress beginning to entertain the French

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to take them in, so one piece is housed inside another

blocks.note: a start is a beginning
le is French for 'the'

explanation.surface: A young actress at the start of her career hosts a party for French guests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginning' looks like a description of the actress's career, but it is the outer piece; French 'le' goes inside it to make STARLET.
explanation.definitionFit: A starlet is a young, ambitious film actress hoping to become a star, so the phrase is a straight synonym.

indicators.note: almost means not quite all of it, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: everyone is ALL, cut short by one letter
feeling down is feeling low

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to disappointing nearly every person they know.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let down' reads as one phrase, but 'Let' is the definition and 'down' supplies its own piece: AL plus LOW gives ALLOW.
explanation.definitionFit: To let someone do something is to permit them, which is exactly what this verb means.

indicators.note: something destroyed is wrecked and its parts scattered, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the twelve letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Mourning fortresses that will shortly be demolished.
explanation.walkthrough: All twelve letters of the two middle words are rearranged; the single word at the start is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone disconsolate is so unhappy that nothing can comfort them, a stronger synonym for being downcast.

clue.text: Those helping you to see detailed plans?

blocks.note: first meaning: informal word for spectacles, eyeglasses
second meaning: short for specifications, technical descriptions

explanation.surface: Who helps you understand the detailed plans of a project?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark hides that 'see' is literal eyesight; the word is short both for spectacles and for specifications.
explanation.definitionFit: The clipped word serves for eyeglasses that improve vision and for written technical specifications describing a design.

indicators.note: a thing following another comes after it, so it is placed second in the line

blocks.note: B is the standard abbreviation for British
an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: A foolish fan trails after a British pop star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'British singer' looks like one phrase, but 'British' gives the letter at the front and 'singer' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A bass is a man who sings in the lowest vocal range, so he is one kind of vocalist.

clue.text: Tale of the middle classes going to and fro

indicators.note: travelling to and fro covers the same ground in both directions, so the word reads the same either way

blocks.note: the definition read whole: a genre of novel about comfortable country families, whose letters run the same both ways

explanation.surface: A story about suburban families who keep commuting back and forth.
explanation.walkthrough: An Aga is a large cast-iron cooking range, a status symbol in British country kitchens; the seven letters read identically forwards and backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a genre of popular British novel about comfortable middle-class domestic life, typically set in rural homes.

blocks.note: first meaning: to separate, end a relationship
second meaning: a port city on the Dalmatian coast

explanation.surface: A couple ends their relationship while on holiday on the Adriatic coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' joins the two meanings; the city's name happens to be an English verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Couples who separate are said to part ways this way, and the same spelling names Croatia's second-largest city.

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the twelve letters taken as written

explanation.surface: China's authorities are furious with the American internet company.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark signals that the definition is an example: Google is one instance of the category.
explanation.definitionFit: Google is the best-known example of a web service that finds pages matching typed keywords.

clue.text: A sailor coming back for reference book

indicators.note: coming back means returning the way one went, so the letters run in the opposite direction

blocks.note: taken as written
an old salt is an experienced sailor

explanation.surface: A seaman returns home to fetch a book he needs to consult.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the sailor turns round; the A stays in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: An atlas is a bound collection of maps that one consults for geography, so it is a kind of reference work.

clue.text: Look at first person reportedly joining dance

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so we go by how it is said rather than spelt

blocks.note: the first person pronoun, spoken, matches the organ of sight
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: Someone eyes up the first guest said to be arriving at the dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First person' is the pronoun I, said aloud as EYE, which then takes BALL to make EYEBALL.
explanation.definitionFit: To eyeball something is an informal verb for staring at it or examining it closely.

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the following word rather than being built

blocks.note: the middle three letters of the African country

explanation.surface: A description of the legal system of an African country.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits in the middle of the country's name, between MA and I.
explanation.definitionFit: The law is the whole body of rules a state enforces, so it collects the statutes and regulations together.

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to take them in, so one piece is let inside the others

blocks.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
a maid is a female domestic servant
B is the chess notation for bishop

explanation.surface: A long-serving housemaid attentively greets the visiting bishop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old maid' looks like the fixed phrase for a spinster, but it splits into O and SERVANT, with B let in between.
explanation.definitionFit: An observant person notices everything around them, so the adjective is a synonym for watchful and alert.

indicators.note: something out of place is disordered, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
the same three-letter word written a second time

explanation.surface: Someone heads off on a journey two times and then takes a flight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' looks like a verb about travelling, but it is the insect; the three-letter word rearranged, written twice, gives TSETSE.
explanation.definitionFit: The tsetse is an African biting insect that spreads sleeping sickness, so it is a particular kind of fly.

clue.text: English chap had to come out

blocks.note: E is the standard abbreviation for English
a chap is a man
to have dinner is to eat it, so had can mean ate

explanation.surface: An Englishman was forced to reveal a secret about himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had to' reads as 'was obliged to', but 'had' means ate and 'to' only joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To emanate is to issue or flow out from a source, as light or smells do.

indicators.note: a gatecrasher forces a way inside uninvited, so one piece pushes into another

blocks.note: H is the standard abbreviation for husband
trash is rubbish

explanation.surface: A married man barges uninvited into a dreadful party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubbish party' reads as a bad party, but 'rubbish' is the outer piece and 'party' alone is the definition; a thrash is informal British slang for a lively party.
explanation.definitionFit: In informal British usage a thrash is a lively celebration or social gathering with plenty of drinking.

clue.text: Old poet, punk at heart, a big hit in the States

definitions.text: a big hit in the States

indicators.note: a thing's heart is its centre, so only the middle letters are kept

blocks.note: Homer was the ancient Greek poet of the Iliad and Odyssey
the two central letters of the word

explanation.surface: An ageing poet with a rebellious streak scores a huge success in America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A big hit' sounds like a success, but it is literal: a baseball hit that lets the batter circle all the bases.
explanation.definitionFit: In baseball, the American national game, a home run is a hit far enough that the batter rounds every base and scores.

clue.text: Doctor a mannerly chap not quite succeeding

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so these letters are altered into a new order

blocks.note: the nine letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A polite physician who never quite makes it to the top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like the subject of the sentence, but it is a verb telling you to rearrange the next nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A nearly man is a British expression for someone who repeatedly comes close to success without ever achieving it.

indicators.note: neglecting at regular intervals means skipping every other letter and keeping the rest

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: The person handing out awards was clearly ignored from time to time.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the odd letters of the long adverb leaves the even ones in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Nobel's will founded the annual prizes for peace, literature and science, so he is the one who endowed them.

clue.text: Immediately providing cover for broadcasters and press

indicators.note: to provide cover for something is to wrap it up and conceal it, so the letters lie hidden inside

blocks.note: letters three to seven of the adverb

explanation.surface: Journalists are quickly given protection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover' suggests news coverage, but here the first word covers the answer inside itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Television, radio and newspapers together make up the mass communication industry, collectively called by this plural noun.

clue.text: Bad actor is a bit of a pig

blocks.note: first meaning: a performer who overacts
second meaning: cured meat from a pig's thigh

explanation.surface: An insult: the poor performer is rather greedy and boorish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit of a pig' reads as 'rather piggish', but it means a literal cut of the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a theatrical overactor and also salted meat from the rear leg of a hog.

blocks.note: a nightmare experience is hell
O is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: A star's ordeal ends with an exclusive story in a glossy magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Hello! is a British weekly glossy that covers celebrity weddings and homes; an over is a set of six balls in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Hello! is a long-running British weekly glossy filled with photographs and gossip about famous people.

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for Bachelor, as in a degree
to stick it out is to endure, to last

explanation.surface: A single man endures to the end of something and then swears.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark splits two sentences; the second word alone is the definition, used as an angry adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words serve as mild swearing adjectives expressing annoyance, as in 'the damn car' or 'the blasted car'.

indicators.note: losing its head means the front is cut off, so the first letter goes

blocks.note: an assassin is a killer

explanation.surface: A hit man grows more unwell after being beheaded.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the K from the hired murderer to leave the comparative ILLER.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative form of ill means more unwell, describing a worsening state of health.

indicators.note: outspoken literally means spoken out loud, so we go by sound rather than spelling

blocks.note: King Lear, Shakespeare's ancient British monarch

explanation.surface: A blunt elderly monarch eyes someone up lewdly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outspoken' sounds like a character trait of the king, but it signals sound; the apostrophe s stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A leer is a sly, suggestive sideways glance that conveys sexual interest or malicious intent.

indicators.note: to admit someone is to let them in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: David Cameron was Britain's Prime Minister from 2010 to 2016
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: An African country's prime minister confesses to nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The PM is not Cameroon's own but a British one, David Cameron; 'admitting' looks like confessing but means letting in.
explanation.definitionFit: Cameroon is a republic in west-central Africa on the Gulf of Guinea, so it is a country there.
